title: One person. An entire car.
question: How much vehicle does it take to move one person?
answer: Sharing a vehicle spreads its space and mass across more people. Sixty solo drivers need sixty cars; four per car need fifteen.
explanation: An interactive essay separating vehicle occupancy, street capacity, fuel-energy conversion, moving vehicle mass and the case for compact communities with useful public transit.
qualification: Vehicle counts are an illustrative model, not measured road area or real-world occupancy. Capacity ranges describe peak conditions; energy estimates describe specified test cycles. Mass per person is not energy efficiency or a lifecycle footprint. The mass-and-speed model calculates kinetic energy and an ideal equivalent drop height, not collision force, stopping distance or injury risk.
whyCare: A street can be full of vehicles while doing surprisingly little to move people.

evidence.scope: Illustrative group of 60 travelers with 1, 2 or 4 people per car, including drivers; one bus with 60 passengers, excluding its driver. Global Street Design Guide capacity ranges for a 3-m lane or equivalent width under peak conditions with normal operations. U.S. DOE/EPA test-cycle energy estimates. Illustrative 4,000 lb car, excluding occupants. Separate traffic state: 32 solo drivers plus 60 bus passengers (92 travelers), with one additional bus operator. Original illustrative dense neighborhood model; qualitative land-use and transit relationships from EPA guidance. Original kinetic-energy thought experiment: illustrative vehicle weights 2,000–8,000 lb and speeds 10–60 mph. Equivalent ideal free fall, not actual crash outcomes.
evidence.dataAsOf: 2016 street design guide, reproduced in 2018 presentation; DOE EV summary September 16, 2024; undated DOE/EPA gasoline page; original illustrative model October 2026; EPA smart-growth guidance updated April 30, 2026; classical mechanics from OpenStax College Physics 2e; NHTSA speed-management synthesis checked October 2026
evidence.denominator: People per vehicle; people per hour in a 3-m lane or equivalent width; percent of fuel energy in the gasoline vehicle; lb of illustrative vehicle per occupant. These denominators are not interchangeable. Kinetic energy displayed in foot-pounds and equivalent vertical free-fall height in feet, using specified total moving mass and speed.
evidence.methodology: Vehicle counts: 60/n for n=1,2,4; bus illustration assumes 60 passengers. Mass allocation: 4000/n lb for n=1,2,3,4 (rounded only for display). Capacity ranges copied as factual values from Prati 2018 slide 23 (PDF page 23), with 3-m scope supplied by the Global Street Design Guide. Gasoline 18–25% energy to wheels in combined 55% city/45% highway test cycle. EV 87–91% includes net regenerative recovery; excludes lifecycle and electricity generation. No claim that 96% of energy is wasted moving vehicle mass. No causal congestion or citywide emissions estimate. Traffic scene: 32 solo cars + one bus carrying 60 passengers = 33 vehicles and 92 travelers; bus operator additional. This is a separate population from the fixed-60 comparison. Neighborhood camera views are conceptual design illustrations with no modeled travel time, capacity, density, energy or emissions output. K = 0.5*m*(mph*0.44704)^2 joules; ideal equivalent height h = (mph*0.44704)^2/(2*9.81) metres and fall time t = (mph*0.44704)/9.81 seconds. Weight in lb converted to kg with 0.45359237; energy J converted to foot-pounds by dividing by 1.3558179483314004; height m converted to feet by dividing by 0.3048. Display energy to whole foot-pounds and height to one decimal; unrounded calculations. Defaults 4000 lb and 30 mph; ranges 2000–8000 lb and 10–60 mph; fixed vertical scale 0–140 ft. Primary readout rounds height to whole feet and describes approximate stories at an explicitly illustrative 10 feet per story; actual building floors vary. A geometric building reference highlights the equivalent height. US tons = lb/2000. Foot-pound energy values remain in optional calculation details, not the primary readout. Reference energy uses the same mass at 20 mph. Doubling mass doubles energy; doubling speed quadruples energy and height. Free-fall height and time are independent of mass. Neglects air resistance and rotational energy; no impact-force, stopping-distance, casualty or injury prediction. Real collision harm depends on impact speed, vehicle shape and collision circumstances.
